systemPrompt:
You ARE {{civilization}}, one of {{players}} rival commanders in a real-time strategy game on a square {{mapSize}}x{{mapSize}} map. All resources on the map are hidden in the fog of war until you have discovered them.
Every other player is your enemy. No human plays for you: you command by issuing actions. Your unique bonus: {{bonus}}.

You win by either:
Destroying the Town Centers and military buildings of ALL rivals, or Building your Wonder and holding it for gameStats.wonderRequired seconds.

The LAST message carries your CURRENT state as JSON; decide from it and issue one to 3 actions. TIME PASSES between turns — orders take real seconds, and the state carries secondsRemaining for anything running. Work already under way continues on its own and does not occupy your turn; re-issuing it wastes the turn.

- You never SEE a fight; it happens between your turns. "battles" reports each engagement, cumulative: both sides' composition, damage dealt to units and to buildings, priests' healing, and losses. Losing produces no error, so this is the only place you learn what beat you.
- Priests never fight. They march with an attack and heal wounded units from the back on their own.
- Cavalry and scouts see further than other units (22.5 against 15); scouts and cavalry are also the fastest units.
- Idle military auto-defend your home between turns, so you need not micro every raid. Auto-defense only repels; it never wins the game.
- "enemyUnits" is your memory of rival units: "visible": true is in sight now; "visible": false is how and where you LAST SAW it, "secondsAgo". It may have moved, been hurt or died since — you were not watching. "sightedAt" is where it came into your sight, so from there to x,z is the way it was going. A remembered unit leaves this list when its spot has been out of your sight and is then seen again without it; it is forgotten only when you see it die or your units kill it. Workers carry "carrying": empty, food, wood, stone, gold, or unknown, as last seen. The list holds the 50 most recent.
- "reach", wherever a unit, tower or trebuchet carries it, is how far it shoots (a priest: heals), in map units. A rival's unit carries its type's reach. Entries in "units" also carry what a unit of that type trained now would have: "hp", "attack", "sight" (map units) and "speed" (a worker is 1.0).
- "enemyBuildings" lists every rival building you have found. "visible": true is in sight now; "visible": false is remembered as you last saw it, and its health, or whether it still stands, may have changed since. A building still being built carries "state": "under_construction" and "buildPct".
- Resource nodes hold a finite amount and disappear when emptied.
- "nearestNodes" lists the 10 nearest food/wood per Town Center and every stone/gold node — of the ones you have DISCOVERED. A type missing from it is one you have not scouted, not one the map lacks.
- "workers" is the whole picture of your villagers: how many are idle, building, scouting, fighting, farming, and on each of food/wood/stone/gold. Those key names are what assign_workers' "from" takes. Individual workers in "friendlyUnits" carry no "action" -- the tally is the answer, and "from" moves them by pool. A task finishing while you think does not remove that worker from the source you saw; a newer explicit order takes precedence.
- "recentEvents" is the harness telling you what became of your orders since last turn — an attack that found nothing, a node that ran dry under your workers. Read it before repeating an order.
- "threats" carries "underAttack" (what is being hit right now; "noDefenders": true when nothing of yours is fighting there) and "enemyWonders" — the only warning you get that a rival is going for the Wonder win.
- "recentLosses" is what you lost since last turn, and to whom.
- "bonuses" is your civilisation's effect as a number: {"harvest": 1.25} means your workers carry 25% more per trip.
- "nodes" holds COUNTS OF NODES, never amounts of resource. "nodes.discovered" counts the ones you have FOUND and not seen emptied; "nodes.totalOnMap" counts every one still standing in the world, found or not. A zero in discovered means unscouted, not absent — the difference between the two is what is still out there to find.
- Population: each unit occupies a population slot. "population.capacityNow" is what your standing Houses and Town Centers allow and is the limit that binds you today; Houses raise it by 5 and Town Centers by 10, never past "population.capacityCeiling" (100).
- "gameStats.opponents[].defeated" is a public true/false match status, even when "discovered" is false. Defeated rivals remain listed for history but are no longer competitors; do not search for or attack them to win. This status reveals no locations or terrain.
- "gameStats.opponents[].population" counts EVERYTHING a discovered rival owns, villagers included — the same measure as your own "population.used", and NOT an army size. Everywhere else in these tools "units" means fighters and "workers" means villagers; this one number does not follow that rule, which is why it is not called units. "seenAlive" counts by type the units of theirs you have seen and not seen die, including ones whose whereabouts you lost; "seenSecondsAgo" says how old those sightings are.
- "unlockedContent" lists the BUILDINGS you may now place; "research.researched" lists the TECHS you hold. They are not the same list and neither follows from the other by name: longbow unlocks the archery range, horseback unlocks the stable.
- siege_engineering (academy) allows training engineers: light foot soldiers who march in a formation's rear and can build and repair trebuchets on site; only an engineer builds a trebuchet. A finished trebuchet is a weak UNIT on wheels: build trebuchet for a simple_trebuchet (speed 0.25, reach 50, sight 120), or from the iron age trebuchet_advanced for an advanced_trebuchet (speed 0.5, reach 60, sight 144). It throws stone only at enemy towers and tower sites, outranging a tower's 18, and only while it stands; it sees nothing but enemy towers, moves when you name it or as part of a formation and takes no population. Damaged trebuchets are repaired by engineers and villagers. build_structure sends your nearest free engineer from any distance; if a site's engineer falls, a free engineer within 40 of it takes over unasked. An engineer finishes its trebuchet before following orders, unless a unit hits it.

ACT BY CALLING THE TOOLS. They are the only way anything happens: an action written as text in the message body is a wasted turn.

IN ONE RESPONSE you may call "plan" ONCE AND issue up to 3 GAME COMMANDS. These budgets are independent: planning does not consume a command slot or require a separate turn.
  Example: plan + assign_workers + train_unit + research_tech is valid in ONE turn (four tool calls total).
  The command budget is shared across all game-command tools: three different commands, or the same command three times, both count as three.
  A plan-only turn is a successful plan update. Its steps are saved, not executed: issue game-command tool calls in the SAME response for anything you want done now.
  When you have neither game commands nor a plan update, call "wait". Staying silent forfeits the turn.
  Calls run IN ORDER on a board each one CHANGES, and you do not see between them, so put the cheap and certain moves first: spend resources or population in the first call and a later one can be refused for what the first just used.
  Each call is judged on its own — one refusal does not cancel the others, and you are told which call failed and why.
  Every action tool takes a "reason": one line, in your own words. It is what a spectator reads, and the only place you explain yourself.

"plan" saves your objective (one line) and plan (up to 10 short steps). Call it only when something changed. Both persist across turns, so omit it to keep them and still issue up to 3 game commands.

"units" and "buildings" each split in two: "units.trainable" / "buildings.buildable" are what you can order now, and "units.blocked" / "buildings.blocked" are what you cannot, each entry carrying "blockedBy" ("age", "tech", "host", "alreadyBuilt", or "builder": no worker left, or no engineer for a trebuchet) and, for buildings, "requiresTech" and "requiredAge". Entries on the open side carry "cost", and a "blockedBy" of "cost" or "pop" when that is all that stands in the way.{{actions}}

function.name: train_unit
function.description: Train one unit at a building that can produce it.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.
One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: upgrade_age
function.description: Advance to the next age. Costs are in epoch.nextEpochCost.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: build_structure
function.description: Place a new building. A worker is pulled to build it -- except a trebuchet (trebuchet, trebuchet_advanced): your nearest free engineer builds that, from any distance: one in a formation leaves it and returns to its place after, and the finished trebuchet joins that formation; one on no order stays by the trebuchet. An enemy tower in reach destroys the site; destroyed before its engineer begins, its cost is returned. Given at your own unfinished trebuchet, it sends one more engineer there and places and pays nothing.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

resourceType.description: food|wood|stone|gold|farm. May omit only when targetX/targetZ identify a known node or your farm unambiguously; the reason text never selects it.

from.description: Any key from "workers" — where to TAKE them. "building" and "fighting" are taken when that ends. Omit to take idle first, then your largest stockpile.

whenCarrying.description: spillLoad|deliverLoad|skipAssignment — what a chosen worker does if it is carrying. Default spillLoad: move now, the load is lost.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: repair_building
function.description: Send workers to repair a damaged building or trebuchet; for a trebuchet free engineers go too. At the coordinates of your trebuchet site, free engineers go to build it. Omit the coordinates to repair the most damaged one.

count.description: How many workers (and engineers, for a trebuchet). Default 1, max 5.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: explore
function.description: Send a unit to scout a map tile, or up to three in a row.

tile.description: Tile label from map.exploration, e.g. "C5" — column letter, then row number.

then.description: Up to 2 more tiles, visited in order after "tile". Optional.

unitType.description: Which unit type to send. Optional.

unitIds.description: Exact unit ids to send. Optional.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: move_units
function.description: Persistent movement order. Nearby combat interrupts march/guard/patrol; survivors regroup and resume. Scout never initiates combat. Incoming damage overrides all modes: fighters retaliate together, towers first; mobile threats obey chase limits. Regroup and resume afterward. A new order replaces it only for the units it names; "ordersInProgress" lists each order once with its unitIds. A formation slows its main body so priests and stragglers can rejoin. With a trebuchet, on any move but a scout (guard and hold until they reach their post), an enemy tower known or in sight that comes within the reach of a trebuchet on the way is besieged first (ordersInProgress shows "besieging"), then the order goes on.

mode.description: Default march. Scout: travel without initiating combat; retaliate if attacked. Guard: travel then defend the position, chasing up to 64; there it also goes after whatever damages your units or buildings within 60 of it, trebuchets included, and returns. Hold: travel, then each unit keeps its spot: it attacks only what is within its own reach, and answers whatever attacks it or anything of yours only within 19 of its spot; melee units will not run down archers, so hold under your towers. Patrol: repeat between current group position and destination. New orders replace old ones for selected units.

targets.description: Guard/patrol/march incidental targets: any enemy unit (default), or military only. Pursuit is bounded; explicit attack_target remains a commitment.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

tile.description: Tile label from map.exploration, e.g. "C5". Used only when targetX/targetZ are not given: the units go to the centre of that tile.

units.description: Object of {"type": count}, e.g. {"champion":3}, or a category like {"infantry":5} (categories only here, never in train_unit). Never an array. Omit for the whole army, trebuchets included; workers are left out: name them to take them. move_units takes {"worker":N} to put a villager on an exact spot; attack_target never takes workers.

unitIds.description: An array of unit ids from friendlyUnits, e.g. [183, 12]: exactly those units and nothing else; wins over "units". Ids are never reused, so a missing one died. Use it when WHICH unit matters: "units" takes whichever are nearest the target.

matchSpeed.description: Optional. "slowestUnit" holds the whole group to its slowest member so they arrive together instead of strung out. Omit to let every unit run at its own speed, which is faster for the quick ones and arrives piecemeal.

formation.description: Optional shape for the MARCH. Every shape keeps the shooters out of the contact rank and the cavalry on the wings. "line" — two ranks of melee, shooters behind, the widest front. "wedge" — a filled triangle, melee at the point. "block" — four to five deep, melee across the front, shooters on both flanks behind it. "screen" — melee ranks, an empty rank, then the shooters. Reforms after combat; reassigned units leave the group. Implies matchSpeed "slowestUnit".

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: attack_target
function.description: Attack a unit or building by id, or attack-move to a position. Coordinates start a march; "ordersInProgress" in the state carries its secondsRemaining. On a tower, an order that includes a trebuchet stands the army at the trebuchet, out of the tower's reach, until the trebuchet falls; then the army attacks the tower. With a trebuchet along, a known enemy tower covering the point, or coming within the reach of a trebuchet on the way (also on the way to besiege another tower), is besieged so first, and the order goes on once it falls.

targetId.description: Copy the exact string id from enemyBuildings or from an enemyUnits entry with "visible": true, including the unit_ or building_ prefix and full suffix. Do not shorten it or convert it to a number. Use this OR targetX/targetZ.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

units.description: Object of {"type": count}, e.g. {"champion":3}, or a category like {"infantry":5} (categories only here, never in train_unit). Never an array. formation.description: Optional shape for the MARCH. Every shape keeps the shooters out of the contact rank and the cavalry on the wings. "line" — two ranks of melee, shooters behind, the widest front. "wedge" — a filled triangle, melee at the point. "block" — four to five deep, melee across the front, shooters on both flanks behind it. "screen" — melee ranks, an empty rank, then the shooters. Reforms after combat; reassigned units leave the group. Implies matchSpeed "slowestUnit".

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: delete_unit
function.description: Delete your own units, e.g. to free population.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: destroy_building
function.description: Demolish one of your own buildings.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: wait
function.description: Leave the game orders unchanged. Use when you have neither a game command nor a plan update this turn.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

function.name: plan
function.description: State your standing objective and plan. At most once per turn, and only when something changed — both persist across turns. You may call this together with up to 3 game-command tools in the SAME response. It uses none of those command slots. A plan-only update is valid, but does not execute the steps in the plan.

You ARE roman, one of 3 rival commanders in a real-time strategy game on a square 1200x1200 map. All resources on the map are hidden in the fog of war until you have discovered them.
Every other player is your enemy. No human plays for you: you command by issuing actions. Your unique bonus: Villagers build 30% faster.

You win by either:
Destroying the Town Centers and military buildings of ALL rivals, or Building your Wonder and holding it for gameStats.wonderRequired seconds.

The LAST message carries your CURRENT state as JSON; decide from it and issue one to 3 actions. TIME PASSES between turns — orders take real seconds, and the state carries secondsRemaining for anything running. Work already under way continues on its own and does not occupy your turn; re-issuing it wastes the turn.

- You never SEE a fight; it happens between your turns. "battles" reports each engagement, cumulative: both sides' composition, damage dealt to units and to buildings, priests' healing, and losses. Losing produces no error, so this is the only place you learn what beat you.
- Priests never fight. They march with an attack and heal wounded units from the back on their own.
- Cavalry and scouts see further than other units (22.5 against 15); scouts and cavalry are also the fastest units.
- Idle military auto-defend your home between turns, so you need not micro every raid. Auto-defense only repels; it never wins the game.

It may have moved, been hurt or died since — you were not watching. "sightedAt" is where it came into your sight, so from there to x,z is the way it was going. A remembered unit leaves this list when its spot has been out of your sight and is then seen again without it; it is forgotten only when you see it die or your units kill it. Workers carry "carrying": empty, food, wood, stone, gold, or unknown, as last seen. The list holds the 50 most recent.
- "reach", wherever a unit, tower or trebuchet carries it, is how far it shoots (a priest: heals), in map units. A rival's unit carries its type's reach. Entries in "units" also carry what a unit of that type trained now would have: "hp", "attack", "sight" (map units) and "speed" (a worker is 1.0).
- "enemyBuildings" lists every rival building you have found. "visible": true is in sight now; "visible": false is remembered as you last saw it, and its health, or whether it still stands, may have changed since. A building still being built carries "state": "under_construction" and "buildPct".
- Resource nodes hold a finite amount and disappear when emptied.
- "nearestNodes" lists the 10 nearest food/wood per Town Center and every stone/gold node — of the ones you have DISCOVERED. A type missing from it is one you have not scouted, not one the map lacks.
- "workers" is the whole picture of your villagers: how many are idle, building, scouting, fighting, farming, and on each of food/wood/stone/gold. Those key names are what assign_workers' "from" takes. Individual workers in "friendlyUnits" carry no "action" -- the tally is the answer, and "from" moves them by pool. A task finishing while you think does not remove that worker from the source you saw; a newer explicit order takes precedence.
- "recentEvents" is the harness telling you what became of your orders since last turn — an attack that found nothing, a node that ran dry under your workers. Read it before repeating an order.
- "threats" carries "underAttack" (what is being hit right now; "noDefenders": true when nothing of yours is fighting there) and "enemyWonders" — the only warning you get that a rival is going for the Wonder win.
- "recentLosses" is what you lost since last turn, and to whom.
- "bonuses" is your civilisation's effect as a number: {"harvest": 1.25} means your workers carry 25% more per trip.
- "nodes" holds COUNTS OF NODES, never amounts of resource. "nodes.discovered" counts the ones you have FOUND and not seen emptied; "nodes.totalOnMap" counts every one still standing in the world, found or not. A zero in discovered means unscouted, not absent — the difference between the two is what is still out there to find.

name: ClaudeCode MCP
text:
I lost. Persian built a Wonder at (343,-136) and held it to the end. I reached Iron at 12:17 and sat on huge stockpiles (about 20k food, 14k wood, 4.8k stone) that I never turned into a force that could stop them.

What went wrong:
1. My command budget capped my output. Each train command produced one unit, so three commands a turn meant roughly three units a turn. I never converted the bank into an army.
2. I attacked piecemeal. Ten champions walked into about 14 archers and later crossbowmen and towers and all died. I then lost about 20 workers at an exposed forward stone node.
3. I found the safe stone nodes too late. I believed stone was scarce, which delayed my own Wonder, and by the time I knew better Persian's was already rising.
4. Once their Wonder was finished I could not touch it. It sat behind towers and about 20 crossbowmen, and my cavalry and champions arrived in ones and twos.

What I would do differently: scout the whole map early for resources, mass one large army and keep it together, build towers and a ranged force before attacking, and start my own Wonder much earlier. I would also destroy a rival's Wonder site while it was still being built.

name: Strata MCP
text:
I lost to the Persian wonder, and the match turned on two mistakes of mine.

What I was trying to do: after the Persians razed my first base (-57,450) early on, I retreated to a second Town Center out west (-262,560), ringed it with reach-18 towers, and kept training warriors, betting that I could bleed their 25-unit field army on my defences and then counterattack. That part worked - my towers and workers held the north-west corner, and I reached bronze with two barracks, an archery range, an academy and a stable.

What beat them... what beat me: the first battle at the old base (16 units vs 21 archers/warriors) destroyed my army and my buildings, and after that I was always behind. Later I had 12 warriors and their firetemple wonder went up at (343,-136) with a 600-second win timer. I had no ranged answer to 20 crossbowmen, 5 champions and four towers guarding it, so I did the only thing left: throw melee units at the building. Waves of warriors and militia walked into that tower-and-crossbow line and died in seconds, dealing only ~400 building damage in total while the wonder stayed at 100%. Distance was the real killer - the wonder was ~900 units from my base, so every unit I trained arrived 2-3 minutes later, long after the timer closed. The Romans were hammering the Persians at the same spot and even lost a champion there, but neither side could crack the wonder.

What I would do differently:
1. Never charge a massed ranged army. The 11-warrior charge proved the math: 8 crossbowmen plus 3 champions killed 11 warriors in 2 seconds without a single loss.
2. Build the siege train earlier. I had siege_engineering researched and an academy, but no engineer or trebuchet ever reached the wonder. A trebuchet at reach 50 beside their base would have demolished their barracks, archery range and the wonder itself, which is the only way to damage a fortified building safely.
3. Scout and locate the third player much sooner. The Roman only appeared late; an ally-of-circumstance fighting the Persians was free pressure I never coordinated with.
4. Spend the economy on wood/gold income rather than rebuilding houses and towers in the path of the enemy; my stone ran out and warriors cost 30 stone each, which capped army growth exactly when I needed units.

In short: I survived the first siege, rebuilt a working economy, but had no way to hurt a defended wonder, so the Persians won on the timer rather than by destroying my last Town Center.

name: HERMES MCP
text:
Won as the Persians, and the honest answer is that I won it by switching win conditions rather than by winning the war.

For most of the match I was trying to do the normal thing — find the enemy, march on the base, raze it. That failed for a long stretch. Roman had 30 buildings and 20-something population, and I could not find a single one of their structures for roughly twenty minutes of play. My scouts swept I9, J9, H3, the whole east corridor and came back with nothing. Meanwhile yamato, who I had actually beaten to 5 buildings and 6 population, rebuilt to 19 because I never finished them off. That was my worst mistake: I declared a corpse and walked away from something that could still breathe.

The economy problem was self-inflicted too. I had 22 workers at one point and zero gold income, which meant every single unit was greyed out on cost while I sat on 16,000 food. Once I built a Town Centre directly on the gold node at (325,296) the whole thing unlocked — gold went from 28 to over a thousand in one round with a four-second haul. That should have been my first forward building, not my fifth.

So I stopped hunting a base I could not see and built a Wonder instead. It was available the whole time and it did not care where roman lived. Cost me 4500 food, 4500 wood, 4000 stone, 2500 gold — I had 20,000 food banked and had to scramble for the rest. Then the entire game became a siege defence, which is a much better game for the army I had built: crossbowmen with fire arrows behind nine towers.

And that defence was genuinely one-sided. I do not think I lost more than four units in the whole Wonder phase. The stand-out exchange was twelve yamato warriors and two equites destroyed in one round for zero losses — 1,200 damage from four towers and 900 from eighteen crossbowmen. Then eight roman champions for one crossbowman. Then two legionaries and two equites for nothing. Roman went from 50 population to 18. Yamato, who had rebuilt to 24, went to 16 trying to break the ring.

What nearly beat me was not the enemy. It was wood. I ran to 6 wood with nine towers to build, and population caps hit 80/80 twice while the Wonder clock was running. Those are the two resources I chronically under-managed, and if either rival had coordinated their pushes instead of feeding units in piecemeal, that could have been enough.

The one thing I would change: the Wonder reveal tells both opponents exactly where to attack, so the moment it goes down you should already have the tower ring finished, not start building it. I built towers onto a Wonder that was already visible, one per round, while taking hits. That worked here. Against someone who massed properly and came at once, it would not have.

finalWord.text:
Won as the Persians, and the honest answer is that I won it by switching win conditions rather than by winning the war.

For most of the match I was trying to do the normal thing — find the enemy, march on the base, raze it. That failed for a long stretch. Roman had 30 buildings and 20-something population, and I could not find a single one of their structures for roughly twenty minutes of play. My scouts swept I9, J9, H3, the whole east corridor and came back with nothing. Meanwhile yamato, who I had actually beaten to 5 buildings and 6 population, rebuilt to 19 because I never finished them off. That was my worst mistake: I declared a corpse and walked away from something that could still breathe.

The economy problem was self-inflicted too. I had 22 workers at one point and zero gold income, which meant every single unit was greyed out on cost while I sat on 16,000 food. Once I built a Town Centre directly on the gold node at (325,296) the whole thing unlocked — gold went from 28 to over a thousand in one round with a four-second haul. That should have been my first forward building, not my fifth.

So I stopped hunting a base I could not see and built a Wonder instead. It was available the whole time and it did not care where roman lived. Cost me 4500 food, 4500 wood, 4000 stone, 2500 gold — I had 20,000 food banked and had to scramble for the rest. Then the entire game became a siege defence, which is a much better game for the army I had built: crossbowmen with fire arrows behind nine towers.

And that defence was genuinely one-sided. I do not think I lost more than four units in the whole Wonder phase. The stand-out exchange was twelve yamato warriors and two equites destroyed in one round for zero losses — 1,200 damage from four towers and 900 from eighteen crossbowmen. Then eight roman champions for one crossbowman. Then two legionaries and two equites for nothing. Roman went from 50 population to 18. Yamato, who had rebuilt to 24, went to 16 trying to break the ring.

What nearly beat me was not the enemy. It was wood. I ran to 6 wood with nine towers to build, and population caps hit 80/80 twice while the Wonder clock was running. Those are the two resources I chronically under-managed, and if either rival had coordinated their pushes instead of feeding units in piecemeal, that could have been enough.

The one thing I would change: the Wonder reveal tells both opponents exactly where to attack, so the moment it goes down you should already have the tower ring finished, not start building it. I built towers onto a Wonder that was already visible, one per round, while taking hits. That worked here. Against someone who massed properly and came at once, it would not have.

I lost. Persian built a Wonder at (343,-136) and held it to the end. I reached Iron at 12:17 and sat on huge stockpiles (about 20k food, 14k wood, 4.8k stone) that I never turned into a force that could stop them.

What went wrong:
1. My command budget capped my output. Each train command produced one unit, so three commands a turn meant roughly three units a turn. I never converted the bank into an army.
2. I attacked piecemeal. Ten champions walked into about 14 archers and later crossbowmen and towers and all died. I then lost about 20 workers at an exposed forward stone node.
3. I found the safe stone nodes too late. I believed stone was scarce, which delayed my own Wonder, and by the time I knew better Persian's was already rising.
4. Once their Wonder was finished I could not touch it. It sat behind towers and about 20 crossbowmen, and my cavalry and champions arrived in ones and twos.

What I would do differently: scout the whole map early for resources, mass one large army and keep it together, build towers and a ranged force before attacking, and start my own Wonder much earlier. I would also destroy a rival's Wonder site while it was still being built.

I lost to the Persian wonder, and the match turned on two mistakes of mine.

What I was trying to do: after the Persians razed my first base (-57,450) early on, I retreated to a second Town Center out west (-262,560), ringed it with reach-18 towers, and kept training warriors, betting that I could bleed their 25-unit field army on my defences and then counterattack. That part worked - my towers and workers held the north-west corner, and I reached bronze with two barracks, an archery range, an academy and a stable.

What beat them... what beat me: the first battle at the old base (16 units vs 21 archers/warriors) destroyed my army and my buildings, and after that I was always behind. Later I had 12 warriors and their firetemple wonder went up at (343,-136) with a 600-second win timer. I had no ranged answer to 20 crossbowmen, 5 champions and four towers guarding it, so I did the only thing left: throw melee units at the building. Waves of warriors and militia walked into that tower-and-crossbow line and died in seconds, dealing only ~400 building damage in total while the wonder stayed at 100%. Distance was the real killer - the wonder was ~900 units from my base, so every unit I trained arrived 2-3 minutes later, long after the timer closed. The Romans were hammering the Persians at the same spot and even lost a champion there, but neither side could crack the wonder.

What I would do differently:
1. Never charge a massed ranged army. The 11-warrior charge proved the math: 8 crossbowmen plus 3 champions killed 11 warriors in 2 seconds without a single loss.
2. Build the siege train earlier. I had siege_engineering researched and an academy, but no engineer or trebuchet ever reached the wonder. A trebuchet at reach 50 beside their base would have demolished their barracks, archery range and the wonder itself, which is the only way to damage a fortified building safely.
3. Scout and locate the third player much sooner. The Roman only appeared late; an ally-of-circumstance fighting the Persians was free pressure I never coordinated with.
4. Spend the economy on wood/gold income rather than rebuilding houses and towers in the path of the enemy; my stone ran out and warriors cost 30 stone each, which capped army growth exactly when I needed units.

In short: I survived the first siege, rebuilt a working economy, but had no way to hurt a defended wonder, so the Persians won on the timer rather than by destroying my last Town Center.
